summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with chest pain, nausea, and vomiting following a dialysis session. Initial concerns for cardiac ischemia were ruled out as troponin levels were mildly elevated but stable and MB negative, with EKG changes attributed to lead placement. A urinary tract infection was diagnosed based on urinalysis and symptoms of dysuria, and treated with cefepime initially, then transitioned to ciprofloxacin. Two painful skin lesions on the inner thigh and left hip were biopsied, confirming calciphylaxis, leading to initiation of sodium thiosulfate therapy and increased dialysis frequency to daily, then planned for four times weekly. Nausea was managed by switching from calcium acetate to lanthanum as a phosphate binder and using antiemetics. Hypertension was addressed with uptitration of isosorbide dinitrate and addition of amlodipine. The chronic abdominal wound showed signs of healing and was deemed stable. The patient was discharged to an extended care facility with plans for ongoing dialysis, dermatology follow-up, and management of multiple comorbidities.
